13735: Gentiles from pagan backgrounds would hear that their whole lives were now worship of the one God, not just occasional temple visits. Jewish believers would recognise Torah and proverbs. Both groups, divided over food and customs, were told to think soberly about themselves and honour one another. Members facing hostility in the city were told not to retaliate.
13736: Romans 12:1-2 is often applied to individual consecration. Its original focus is the community: one body, many gifts, mutual honour. Its call to bless persecutors and refuse revenge remains one of the most demanding ethical teachings in the New Testament.
13737: God desires a broken and contrite heart more than animal sacrifice.
13738: 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay', quoted in Rom 12:19.
13739: Feed your hungry enemy and heap burning coals on his head, quoted in Rom 12:20.
13740: Do not take vengeance; love your neighbour as yourself: the Torah root of Paul's ethic.
13741: Romans 12:1-2 is mainly about each individual's private dedication and finding God's personal will for my life.
13742: It is personal, but Paul's plurals point to a community offering itself together, and 'God's will' is spelled out in the rest of the chapter: humility, gifts used for others, genuine love and peace with enemies.
13743: Rulers, Taxes and the Debt of Love
13744: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, since all authority exists under God, and rulers are God's servants to reward good and punish wrong. They should pay taxes and give respect and honour where due. The only debt they should keep owing is love, because love fulfils the Law. The night is far gone and the day is near, so they should put off the works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
13745: Nero became emperor in AD 54; his early reign was regarded as relatively good. But Jewish communities in Rome had been expelled under Claudius only a few years earlier, so a minority group had good reason to avoid trouble. Tacitus (Annals 13.50-51) records public protests in AD 58 over abuses by indirect tax collectors. Paul distinguishes direct tribute (phoros) and indirect taxes (telos), urging payment of both (13:7). Jewish revolutionary feeling against Rome was also growing in Judea, leading to war in AD 66.
13746: Roman society was a ladder of honour from the emperor down. Paul's 'honour to whom honour is due' (13:7) uses that system. The 'sword' (13:4) symbolised the governor's power to execute. Paul's language of rulers as God's 'servants' (diakonoi, leitourgoi) quietly places Caesar under God, not above him. Night-time drunkenness and revelry (13:13) was common at Roman banquets.
13747: Jewish tradition taught that God gives kingdoms to whom he will (Dan 2:21; Dan 4:17) and that exiles should seek the welfare of the city where they live (Jer 29:7). Jews in the empire prayed and sacrificed for the emperor rather than to him. Daniel also shows the limit: when a king demands worship, faithful Jews refuse (Dan 3; Dan 6). Paul's summary of the commandments in love of neighbour quotes Leviticus 19:18, as Jesus and Rabbi Hillel did in different ways. 'The day is near' reflects the Jewish hope of the day of the Lord.
13748: Jewish believers, remembering the expulsion, would hear a call to be peaceable and give Rome no excuse. Gentile believers, who had abandoned civic gods and might be suspected of disloyalty, would hear that faith in Jesus did not make them rebels. Everyone would hear that their deepest loyalty and 'debt' was love, under a Lord whose day was coming.
13749: Romans 13 calls Christians to be good citizens: pay taxes, respect order, avoid needless conflict. It does not teach that whatever a government commands is right. Rulers are described as servants for good; when they command evil, believers follow Peter: 'We must obey God rather than men' (Acts 5:29). The passage was misused in Nazi Germany and apartheid South Africa, and Christians in both contexts appealed to the wider Bible to resist.
13750: Seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile: the model for minority life under empire.
13751: The Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will.
13752: Three Jews refuse the king's idol: the limit of submission.
13753: Love your neighbour as yourself, quoted in Rom 13:9.
13754: Romans 13 means Christians must always obey the government, since every government is put there by God.
13755: Paul urges a vulnerable minority to be peaceable, pay taxes and honour rulers, while describing rulers as God's servants for good, accountable to God. The rest of Scripture shows that when rulers demand sin or idolatry, God's people obey God. Both Wright and Moo agree it is not a blank cheque.
13756: The Strong and the Weak: Do Not Despise or Judge
13757: Paul addresses divisions over food and holy days. Some eat anything; others, 'weak in faith', eat only vegetables. Some treat one day as special; others treat all days alike. Each must be fully convinced in their own mind, because each lives and dies to the Lord. Do not judge or despise one another; do not destroy for the sake of food someone for whom Christ died. The kingdom of God is not eating and drinking but righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
13758: Many scholars think this chapter reveals the concrete situation behind Romans. The 'weak' were probably mostly Jewish believers (and Gentiles influenced by them) who kept kosher food laws and Sabbath and avoided meat that might have been offered to idols or not slaughtered properly; in Rome, kosher meat may have been hard to obtain, so vegetables were the safe option. The 'strong' were mostly Gentiles (and Jews like Paul) who felt free to eat. Mark Nanos argues instead that the 'weak' were non-Christian Jews in the synagogues where believers still met; most scholars have not followed him, but his reading highlights the Jewish setting.
13759: Shared meals defined community and status in the ancient world. Who you ate with showed whose group you belonged to. For Jews in the diaspora, food laws and Sabbath were key marks of loyalty to God, and Roman writers often mocked them for it. For Gentiles, refusing meat at a civic banquet could be seen as antisocial. Paul applies honour language: the strong should not 'despise' (look down on); the weak should not 'judge' (condemn).
13760: Food laws (Lev 11) and Sabbath (Exod 20:8-11) were part of God's covenant with Israel, and Jewish martyrs had died rather than eat pork (Dan 1:8 and 2 Maccabees 6-7). Paul does not mock this. He says these practices can be done 'to the Lord' (14:6). He also says 'nothing is unclean in itself' (14:14), a statement scholars read differently: as relativising food laws for all believers, or (within the Paul within Judaism view) as addressing Gentiles only. The quotation 'every knee shall bow' (Isa 45:23) reminds both sides that the one God, not they, is judge.
13761: Jewish believers who kept the food laws heard Paul defend their right to do so and forbid others from despising them. Gentile believers who ate freely heard that their freedom must yield to love. Both heard that the kingdom of God is not about food. The goal was that they could actually eat together.
13762: Churches still divide over 'disputable matters': alcohol, worship styles, holidays, diet, cultural customs. Romans 14 gives a pattern: hold convictions sincerely, do not despise or condemn those who differ, limit your freedom for the sake of a weaker brother or sister, and keep the kingdom's priorities.
13763: Israel's food laws distinguished clean and unclean as part of being holy.
13764: Daniel refuses the king's food to avoid defilement, a model for diaspora Jews and the 'weak' who ate vegetables.
13765: Every knee will bow and every tongue confess to God, quoted in Rom 14:11.
13766: The Sabbath commandment, behind the dispute over days.
13767: The 'weak' are immature Christians with legalistic hang-ups, and the 'strong' are mature believers who understand grace.
13768: The 'weak' were most likely faithful Jewish believers keeping God's commands in Torah, and Gentiles who joined them. Paul refuses to let them be despised and asks the strong to bend. Calling them 'legalists' imports a later caricature of Judaism.
13769: Welcome One Another: Jerusalem, Rome and Spain
13770: The strong should bear with the weak and please their neighbour, as Christ did not please himself. Paul prays that they will glorify God 'with one voice' and urges: welcome one another as Christ welcomed you. Christ became a servant to the circumcised to confirm God's promises to the patriarchs, and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy; Paul quotes a chain of scriptures where the nations praise God with Israel. Then he explains his mission: he has preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum, and plans to visit Rome on the way to Spain, after taking a collection from Macedonia and Achaia to the poor believers in Jerusalem.
13771: The collection for Jerusalem was a major project of Paul's later ministry (1 Cor 16:1-4; 2 Cor 8-9). Gentile churches sent money to the Jewish mother church as a sign of unity and gratitude. Paul feared opposition in Judea (15:31), and Acts records that he was arrested in Jerusalem (Acts 21). He wanted Rome to be a base for a mission to Spain, a region at the western edge of the known world, with fewer Jewish communities and little Greek; he would need Roman help with contacts, language and support.
13772: Paul uses benefaction language: the Gentiles have shared in the Jews' spiritual blessings, so they owe it to them to serve them materially (15:27). This is reciprocity in a patronage culture, but flowing from the Gentile periphery to the Jewish centre. Being 'sent on' (propempō, 15:24) meant being supplied for a journey: food, money, companions. Paul describes his ministry as 'priestly service' (hierourgeō), offering the Gentiles as an acceptable offering.
13773: Paul's mission is Israel's mission: the prophets foresaw the nations coming to Zion with gifts and worshipping Israel's God (Isa 60:5-6; Isa 66:20). The quotations in 15:9-12 come from all parts of Israel's scriptures (Psalms, Torah and Prophets) and climax with Isaiah 11:10: the root of Jesse will rise to rule the nations, and in him the nations will hope. Christ is described as a servant to the circumcised for the sake of God's truthfulness (faithfulness) to the patriarchs. The whole letter has been leading here: Jew and Gentile worshipping together as the prophets promised.
13774: Jewish believers heard Christ honoured as the servant who confirmed God's promises to their fathers. Gentile believers heard that their inclusion fulfils Israel's scriptures, and that they owe a debt to Jerusalem. All were asked to welcome one another and to join Paul's mission to Spain and his prayers for Jerusalem.
13775: Romans 15:7 is a fitting summary of the whole letter: welcome one another as Christ welcomed you, for God's glory. Unity across ethnic and cultural lines is not an optional extra but the fulfilment of the gospel. The collection also shows practical, financial solidarity between churches of different cultures.
13776: 'The reproaches of those who reproached you fell on me', applied to Christ in Rom 15:3.
13777: I will praise you among the nations, quoted in Rom 15:9.
13778: Rejoice, O nations, with his people, quoted in Rom 15:10.
13779: The root of Jesse rises to rule the nations; in him they will hope (Rom 15:12).
13780: Those who were not told will see: Paul's reason for preaching where Christ was not yet named (Rom 15:21).
13781: Romans 15-16 are a practical postscript with travel plans and greetings, not part of the letter's real message.
13782: Many scholars (Wright, Jewett, McKnight in *Reading Romans Backwards*) argue the opposite: these chapters show what the whole letter is for. Jews and Gentiles glorifying God together, supporting a mission and sharing resources, is the gospel lived out.
13783: Phoebe, Junia and the Household of God
13784: Paul commends Phoebe, a deacon (diakonos) of the church at Cenchreae and a patron (prostatis) of many, including Paul, who carries the letter. He greets about 26 named people in Rome and several households and house churches, including Prisca and Aquila, his co-workers, and Andronicus and Junia, 'prominent among the apostles'. He warns against those who cause divisions, sends greetings from his companions (including Tertius, the scribe, and Gaius, his host), and closes with praise to God who has revealed the long-hidden mystery for the obedience of faith among all nations.
13785: Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Phoebe probably travelled to Rome, carried the letter and may well have read or explained it to the house churches, as letter carriers often did. Prisca and Aquila, Jews expelled from Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2), had returned and hosted a church. Peter Lampe's study of the names suggests a socially mixed group: many names are typical of slaves or freedpeople, some are Jewish (Paul calls Andronicus, Junia and Herodion his 'kinsfolk'), and several are women. There are textual questions about the ending: some manuscripts place the doxology (16:25-27) after chapter 14 or 15, and a few scholars once argued chapter 16 was sent to Ephesus, but most now accept it as part of Romans.
13786: A prostatis was a patron or benefactor: someone with resources and standing who protected and supported others. Phoebe's role gave her honour and authority, and Paul's commendation asks Rome to receive her 'in a way worthy of the saints'. House churches met in homes (16:5) or in households like those of Aristobulus and Narcissus (16:10-11), possibly slaves and freedpeople of those great families. The 'holy kiss' was a sign of family belonging. Women are named as co-workers and hard workers: Prisca, Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, Julia.
13787: Paul names his Jewish 'kinsfolk' with honour, showing Jewish believers as part of the Roman church's foundation. The promise that 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet' (16:20) echoes Gen 3:15, the first promise of victory over the serpent: Paul's story of Adam (Rom 5) ends in hope. The closing doxology speaks of the mystery revealed through the prophetic writings, so that all nations may come to the obedience of faith, bracketing the letter with 1:5.
13788: Hearers would listen for their own names. Being greeted publicly by an apostle was a mark of honour. Jews and Gentiles, women and men, slaves and free, heard themselves named together as one family. The warning against divisive people (16:17-18) would remind them of the tensions Paul had addressed.
13789: Romans 16 is often skipped, but it shows that Paul's theology was lived in real relationships. It challenges assumptions about women's roles: Phoebe as deacon and patron, Junia as 'prominent among the apostles' (the meaning of this phrase is debated: 'well known to the apostles' or 'outstanding as apostles'). It reminds churches that the gospel creates a diverse family.
13790: The serpent's head will be crushed: echoed in 'the God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet' (Rom 16:20).
13791: All nations stream to the Lord's house: the vision behind a church of many nations.
13792: God as revealer of mysteries, behind the 'mystery kept secret for long ages' (Rom 16:25).
13793: Romans 16 is just a list of names with no teaching value, and its women are helpers rather than leaders.
13794: The list reveals who the church was: Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, women in recognised roles. Phoebe is a deacon and patron who carries the letter; Junia is likely a woman apostle. Scholars debate how these roles relate to later church offices (Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace argue for 'well known to the apostles'; Moo and Schreiner accept 'prominent among the apostles' but take 'apostle' in the looser sense of a travelling missionary), but all agree women were significant in the Roman churches.
13795: 'Works of the law': good deeds in general, or Torah marks of Jewish identity?
13796: When Paul says no one is justified by 'works of the law' (Rom 3:20, 3:28), he means no one can earn heaven by being good. Judaism (and every religion) teaches salvation by human effort; Christianity alone teaches grace.
13797: E. P. Sanders (*Paul and Palestinian Judaism*, 1977) showed that ancient Judaism generally understood itself as a people chosen by grace, keeping Torah as a response within the covenant ('covenantal nomism'). James Dunn and N. T. Wright argue that 'works of the law' in Romans focuses on the Torah as a whole, especially practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath). Paul's target is the idea that membership in God's people is defined by Torah observance, which would exclude Gentiles. See Rom 3:29: 'Or is God the God of Jews only?'
13798: Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner, Stephen Westerholm (*Perspectives Old and New on Paul*, 2004) and Simon Gathercole (*Where Is Boasting?*, 2002) answer that Paul broadens the point: in Romans 4:4-5 he contrasts 'one who works' and receives wages with one who trusts God 'who justifies the ungodly', which sounds like any human doing. The volumes edited by D. A. Carson and others, *Justification and Variegated Nomism* (2001), argue that Second Temple Judaism was more varied than Sanders allowed and included a role for obedience in final salvation. Both sides now agree the old 'legalistic Jews' caricature is wrong, and many hold that Paul's point includes both the boundary markers and the wider truth that no human doing earns God's favour.
13799: If 'works of the law' only means 'trying to be good', Romans can sound anti-Jewish and loses its social target: one table for Jews and Gentiles. If it only means 'boundary markers', Romans can lose its word to every human heart about grace for the ungodly. Reading both together guards against both errors.
13800: 'The righteousness of God': a gift transferred, or God's own covenant faithfulness?
13801: God's righteousness is the perfect moral record God credits to believers. At conversion my sins go to Christ and his righteousness comes to me, so God sees me as righteous.
13802: In Israel's scriptures 'God's righteousness' often means God's saving faithfulness to his promises (Ps 98:2-3; Isa 51:5-8). N. T. Wright reads Rom 1:17 and 3:21-26 mainly as God's covenant faithfulness: God keeps his promise to Abraham and deals with sin through the Messiah. Ernst Käsemann and the apocalyptic school read it as God's saving power invading a world held by sin. Douglas Campbell (*The Deliverance of God*, 2009) stresses God's liberating act rather than a legal transaction.
13803: Reformed and Lutheran scholars (Moo, Schreiner, Westerholm, Mark Seifrid) agree God's righteousness includes his saving action, but argue that in Rom 3:21-22, 4:3-6 and 5:17 Paul also speaks of a righteous status God gives as a gift, and in 2 Cor 5:21 and Phil 3:9 of a righteousness 'from God'. Imputation (God crediting righteousness) is drawn from the 'counting' language of Rom 4. Many argue it is both/and: God's faithful saving act results in a new standing for believers.
13804: The phrase decides whether Romans is mainly about how I get right with God, or mainly about how God is proved faithful in rescuing a people and a world. Most careful readers now hold both: God is faithful, and his faithfulness gives sinners a new standing.
13805: 'Faith in Christ' or 'the faithfulness of Christ' (pistis Christou)?
13806: Rom 3:22 means righteousness comes 'through faith in Jesus Christ'. The focus is my act of believing.
13807: The Greek phrase pistis Iēsou Christou can be read 'faith in Jesus Christ' (objective genitive) or 'the faith(fulness) of Jesus Christ' (subjective genitive: Jesus' own faithful obedience to death). Richard Hays (*The Faith of Jesus Christ*, 1983), Wright, Campbell and others argue for the second: Rom 3:22 would then say God's righteousness is revealed through the Messiah's faithfulness 'for all who believe', which avoids saying 'faith' twice. Rom 5:19 speaks of Christ's obedience in parallel.
13808: James Dunn (on the 'faith in' side, notably), Moo, Schreiner and Westerholm argue that Paul elsewhere uses pistis overwhelmingly for human faith, that Rom 4 makes Abraham's faith the model, and that the repetition is emphatic, not redundant. Early Greek-speaking readers largely took it as 'faith in'. Both readings affirm that Christ's obedience saves and that people must trust him; the dispute is about what this phrase emphasises.
13809: If it is Christ's faithfulness, Romans puts the spotlight first on what Jesus did, not on the quality of my believing, which can free anxious believers. If it is faith in Christ, Paul stresses that the benefit is received by trust alone. Either way, popular teaching that makes faith a work of its own misses Paul.
13811: Romans 7:14-25 describes the mature Christian: I want to do good but keep failing. This is the normal Christian life until heaven, and the more mature I am, the more I feel it.
13812: Werner Georg Kümmel (1929) argued that the 'I' is a rhetorical figure (speech-in-character, prosopopoeia), not Paul's present autobiography. Many modern scholars, including the Reformed scholar Douglas Moo as well as Wright and Stanley Stowers, read the 'I' as Israel under the Law, or Adam, or a person under the Law without the Spirit. Rom 7:14 says 'sold under sin', while Rom 6:18 says believers are 'freed from sin', and Rom 8:2 announces that freedom. Krister Stendahl warned that the West read Paul through its own 'introspective conscience'.
13813: Augustine (later in life), Luther, Calvin, and modern Reformed writers such as J. I. Packer and John Piper read Rom 7 as the believer's ongoing struggle: only the regenerate 'delight in the law of God' (Rom 7:22), and present tenses are used. Dunn holds a mixed view: the believer lives in the overlap of the ages. Scholars on both sides agree that Rom 8 is Paul's goal and that Rom 7 must not be used to excuse sin.
13814: If Rom 7 is the normal Christian life, believers may expect defeat. If it describes life under the Law without the Spirit, Rom 8 becomes the norm: real struggle, but with hope and power. Either reading should send readers to Rom 8, not stop at 7:24.
13816: Romans 9 is mainly about God choosing which individuals go to heaven and which do not, before they are born (Jacob loved, Esau hated; the potter and the clay).
13817: Romans 9-11 answers a question raised by Romans 8: if God's promises are sure, what about Israel? Paul retells Israel's story (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Exodus, prophets) to show God's promise has always moved by his free calling and mercy. 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated' quotes Mal 1:2-3, about the nations Israel and Edom. Wright, Dunn and many Arminian and Wesleyan readers stress corporate and historical election to a role; the chapters end not with fixed reprobation but with mercy on all (Rom 11:32).
13818: John Piper (*The Justification of God*, 1983), Schreiner and Moo argue that Paul's argument does concern individual salvation: the problem is that individual Israelites are 'accursed' (Rom 9:3), and corporate groups are made of individuals. Schreiner notes that corporate and individual election are not opposites. Augustine and Calvin read it this way. The debate is real and long-standing, not a popular misunderstanding.
13819: Pulling Rom 9 out of its story turns a chapter about God's faithfulness to Israel into an abstract debate about predestination only. Reading it within Rom 9-11 keeps both Paul's anguish for his people and his confidence in God's mercy.
13820: Romans 11: has the church replaced Israel?
13821: Since most Jews rejected Jesus, the church is now the 'new Israel' and God's promises to the Jewish people have passed to Christians (often called replacement theology or supersessionism).
13822: Paul says the opposite to Gentile believers who were starting to think so: God has not rejected his people (Rom 11:1-2); Gentiles are wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree and must not boast over the natural branches (Rom 11:17-24); 'the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable' (Rom 11:29). Mark Nanos and the 'Paul within Judaism' school, along with many Catholic and Protestant scholars since the Holocaust, stress Israel's ongoing election.
